Eosinophilic Gastritis: Burden of Disease, Diagnostic Challenges and Unmet Needs
  • Source: Rothenberg ME, et al. Gut 2026;0:1–12
  • Topic: Eosinophilic gastritis (EoG) - rare chronic GI disease with type 2 inflammation
  • Author(s): Rothenberg ME, Chehade M, Dellon ES, Collins M, Talley NJ, Louisias M, Bansal A
Overview of Eosinophilic Gastritis
  • Rare chronic disease --> characterized by pathological eosinophilia of stomach + GI symptoms
  • Pathophysiology: triggered by food antigens --> driven by type 2 immune dysregulation
  • Upregulation of IL-4 and IL-13
  • Diagnosis: symptoms + endoscopic evaluation + abnormal gastric biopsies (dense eosinophilic infiltration)
  • No FDA-approved treatments currently exist
  • Existing options (dietary elimination, off-label corticosteroids) have suboptimal outcomes or inappropriate for long-term use
  • Ongoing clinical trials of biologics --> potential to impact care
Nomenclature (2022 Consensus)
  • EGID preferred umbrella term for GI diseases with pathological eosinophilic infiltration
  • Subdivisions:
  • EoE --> oesophageal involvement
  • EoG --> stomach involvement
  • EoN/EoD/EoJ --> small bowel (jejunum/duodenum)
  • EoC --> colon involvement
  • Non-EoE EGIDs = EoG + EoN + EoC collectively
Epidemiology
  • Prevalence: 5.1–6.3 cases/100,000 (US administrative databases)
  • Overall prevalence of non-EoE EGIDs in patients with GI symptoms: 2% (meta-analysis of 10 studies, 13,377 participants)
  • 43% of patients with moderate-to-severe unexplained abdominal symptoms met criteria for EoG and/or EoD
  • Prevalence appears --> ↑ with age, especially in females:
  • Females <20 years: 4.4 cases/100,000
  • Females 20–64 years: 7.7 cases/100,000
  • Females 60–64 years: 14.4 cases/100,000
  • Sex/gender distribution: no significant differences found in population-based data
  • Likely underdiagnosed due to:
  • Limited disease awareness
  • Misdiagnoses
  • Diagnostic delay (non-specific symptoms)
  • Lack of diagnostic guidelines
  • Terminology confusion
Contributing Factors to Underdiagnosis
  • Symptoms overlap with other GI conditions
  • Normal endoscopic appearance in >60% of patients
  • Non-specific symptoms delay referral
Aetiology and Pathogenesis
Genetic Factors
  • >50% of EGID patients have family history of atopic disease (asthma, food allergy)
  • EoG may be concurrent with EoE (has known genetic determinants)
  • Monogenic diseases can include eosinophilic gastric infiltration:
  • STAT3 deficiency (autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome)
Food Allergen Role
  • EoG driven by dysregulated allergen immune response
  • Evidence from mouse models: oral allergen exposure induces eosinophilic GI responses
  • Elemental diet study: all patients achieved complete histologic remission (<30 eos/hpf) in stomach + duodenum
  • Improvements observed in: symptomatic, endoscopic, QoL, and molecular measures
  • Food oral immunotherapy can cause EoE as adverse effect
  • Case reports of EoG following egg, wheat, milk oral immunotherapies
Type 2 Immune Mechanisms
  • Th2-associated inflammation drives disease (especially in children)
  • Key cytokines upregulated: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13
  • Eotaxin-3 (CCL26) elevated in gastric tissue
  • Regulatory T lymphocytes and Th2 lymphocytes elevated in paediatric patients
  • Gastric Th2 cells strongly correlated with:
  • Peak gastric eosinophil numbers
  • Histopathological features of EoG
Key Differentiating Transcripts (EoG vs EoE)
  • CCL26 (eotaxin-3) - most strongly associated
  • DUOXA2 (dual oxidase maturation factor 2)
  • CDH26 (cadherin-26)
Blood Eosinophil Correlations
  • Blood eosinophilia often elevated in EoG patients
  • 1.09±0.88 × 10³ K/µl in EoG vs 0.09±0.08 K/µl in controls (p=0.0027)
  • Strong correlation with peak gastric biopsy eosinophil count (Pearson r²=0.81, p<0.0001)
Mast Cell Involvement
  • Mast cells increased and activated in gastric/duodenal biopsies of EoG patients vs controls
  • Upregulated mast cell transcripts include:
  • Carboxypeptidase A3
  • Tryptase alpha/beta 1 / tryptase beta 2
  • Hematopoietic prostaglandin D2 synthase
Atopic Comorbidities
  • 57% of adults/children with EoG have ≥1 atopic comorbidity:
  • Food allergy: 29%
  • Asthma: 27%
  • Allergic rhinitis: 24%
  • Atopic dermatitis: 13%
  • US claims database: 39% had ≥1 coexisting allergic condition
Clinical Presentation
Common Presenting Symptoms
  • Abdominal pain
  • Cramping
  • Bloating
  • Early satiety
  • Nausea and vomiting
Subtypes (Klein Classification by Layer Depth)
Subtype Depth of Eosinophilic Infiltration Clinical Course
Mucosal (most common: 88–100%) Mucosa Persistent symptoms
Muscular Muscle layer Frequent relapses
Serosal (rare) Serosa Single flare-ups, long disease-free periods
Mucosal Disease Features
  • Diarrhoea, malabsorption, weight loss
  • Protein-losing enteropathy (from EoD/EoN involvement)
  • Secondary to malabsorption:
  • Iron deficiency
  • Malnutrition
  • Anaemia
  • Hypoalbuminaemia
Muscular Layer Involvement
  • Can lead to gastric outlet obstruction
Serosal Disease Features (Rare)
  • Eosinophilic ascites
  • Peripheral eosinophilia
  • Peritonitis, perforation
  • Pleural effusion
Overlap with Other Conditions

Clinical manifestations may overlap with:

  • Functional dyspepsia
  • Irritable bowel syndrome
  • Bleeding ulcers
  • Malnutrition
Concurrent EGID Involvement
  • 41% of EoG patients also had eosinophilic inflammation of oesophagus
  • 60% of EoG patients diagnosed with another EGID concurrently:
  • 9 patients had: oesophagus (n=7), duodenum (n=1), jejunum (n=3)
Diagnosis
Diagnostic Challenges
  • Symptoms are non-specific and heterogeneous
  • Overlap with other common GI diseases
  • >60% of patients have normal endoscopic appearance
  • Requires high level of suspicion
  • Endoscopists need to suspect diagnosis in appropriate clinical setting
Diagnostic Criteria Summary

1. GI symptoms present

2. Endoscopic evaluation performed

3. Biopsy-confirmed eosinophilic infiltration

4. Exclusion of other causes of GI eosinophilia

Diagnostic Thresholds (Pooled Analysis)
  • Optimal threshold: 20 eos/hpf in 5 gastric hpfs or 33 eos in 1 hpf
  • Higher specificity achieved with higher counts
  • Paediatric threshold: ≥30 eos/hpf in one gastric hpf
  • Some clinical trials used ≥30 eos/hpf in ≥5 hpfs for enrollment
Endoscopic Features
  • Erosion/ulceration
  • Granularity
  • Raised lesions
  • Erythema
  • Friability/bleeding
  • Folds
  • Pyloric stenosis
  • Normal appearance in >60% of patients
Biopsy Recommendations
  • Minimum 4 antral + 4 body biopsies (adults)
  • Include both normal and abnormal appearing mucosa
  • Label each segment in separate containers
  • Communicate high suspicion to pathologist
  • 8 gastric + 4 duodenal biopsies required to capture 100% of cases
Histological Features
  • Eosinophilic infiltration with significantly higher counts vs controls
  • Eosinophils found across full depth of mucosa in EoG
  • In healthy controls: eosinophils confined to deep lamina propria
  • Patchy distribution of EoG requires multiple random biopsies per segment
Eosinophilic Gastritis Histology Scoring System (EoGHSS)

Assesses and grades:

  • Lamina propria eosinophil sheets
  • Periglandular circumferential collars
  • Eosinophils in surface epithelium
  • Eosinophil glandulitis
  • Eosinophil gland abscess (uncommon)
  • Eosinophils in muscularis mucosa/submucosa
  • Lamina propria fibroplasia
  • Lamina propria smooth muscle hyperplasia
  • Reactive epithelial change
  • Acute inflammatory cells (uncommon)
  • Surface erosion and ulceration (uncommon)
Differential Diagnoses to Rule Out
  • Inflammatory bowel disease
  • Coeliac disease
  • Malignancy
  • H. pylori gastritis
  • Collagenous gastritis
  • Atrophic metaplastic autoimmune gastritis
  • Primary hypereosinophilic syndrome
  • Intestinal parasite infections
Diagnostic Yield Factors
  • Higher yield with:
  • Peripheral eosinophilia
  • Hypoalbuminaemia
  • These features should prompt strong consideration of EoG regardless of endoscopic appearance
Diagnostic Delay
  • Average 3.6 years between symptom presentation and diagnosis
  • Contributing factors:
  • Lack of diagnostic guidelines (adults)
  • Limited disease awareness
  • Delayed gastroenterologist referral
  • Delayed oesophagogastroduodenoscopy
  • Lack of biopsy collection/histopathological evaluation
  • No standardised tissue eosinophil count thresholds
  • Failure to document eosinophil counts in pathology reports
Burden of Disease
GI Symptoms
  • Abdominal pain, cramping, bloating
  • Early satiety, nausea, vomiting
Long-term Complications
  • Erosions and ulcers
  • Gastric outlet obstruction
  • GI bleeding
  • Hypoproteinaemia
  • Anaemia
  • Nutritional deficiencies
Growth and Nutrition Impact
  • Impaired growth in children from food avoidance/altered intake
  • Malnutrition in adults
  • Impact on:
  • Bone health
  • Muscle mass
  • Gut microbiome
Quality of Life Impact
  • Significantly impacts health-related QoL
  • Paediatric EGID: QoL scores worse than other paediatric chronic diseases
  • Patient challenges (from surveys):
  • Lack of specialised medical care
  • Financial burden
  • Negative social consequences
  • Emotional burden
Specific QoL Domains Affected
  • Emotional and mental well-being
  • Social functioning
  • Ability to engage in food-related activities
  • Body image perception
  • Sleep
Psychosocial Concerns
  • Fatigue and isolation commonly reported
  • Treatment burden contributes to patient burden
  • Mental health disorders common in adults and children:
  • Anxiety
  • Depression
Economic Burden
  • Healthcare resource utilisation significantly higher in EoG patients vs non-EoG
  • Estimated US healthcare costs: >US$100 million (inflation-adjusted)
  • Costs extrapolated for EoG/EGE and EoC to US population
Treatment Options
Current Status
  • No FDA or EMA approved treatments for EoG
  • No consensus guidelines for adults (in development)
  • ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN guidelines exist for childhood non-EoE EGIDs
Treatment Goals
  • Resolution of symptoms
  • Improvement in endoscopic abnormalities
  • Improvement in histological abnormalities
  • In children: normal growth/development + prevent complications
Treatment Selection Factors
  • Affected segment and depth of inflammation
  • Patient characteristics:
  • Age
  • Clinical presentation
  • Nutritional status
  • Comorbidities
  • Family considerations
Corticosteroid Therapy
Systemic Corticosteroids
  • Mainstay of therapy for EoG in adults and children
  • Based on expert opinion + paediatric guidelines
  • No well-designed scientific studies to support use
  • Induction dose: 0.5–1.0 mg/kg/day, max 40 mg/day
  • Doses not standardised
  • Duration of therapy not determined
Side Effects and Limitations
  • Must be tapered to reduce side effects
  • Side effects limit long-term use
  • Many patients require long-term prednisone (5–10 mg/day) to maintain remission
Relapse Patterns
  • Symptoms typically relapse on cessation of therapy
  • Some cases: sustained remission after discontinuation
  • Retrospective data:
  • 13/21 patients required long-term prednisone (5–10 mg/day)
  • Most switched from PPI or antihistamine after unsuccessful treatment
Topical Corticosteroids (Enteric Budesonide)
  • Alternative with theoretically lower adverse effect risk
  • Dose range: 3–9 mg/day
  • Higher dosage often initiated, then tapered to maintenance dose
  • Administration: capsules opened, granules crushed + mixed with vehicle (apple sauce)
  • Data limited to case reports/series
  • Varying levels of efficacy reported
Steroid-Sparing Approaches
  • Azathioprine may be beneficial in steroid-dependent patients
  • Concomitant dietary restriction/elimination therapy
Dietary Interventions
Types of Dietary Therapy
  • Amino acid-based elemental diets
  • Elimination diets excluding common disease-triggering foods
Elemental Diet Evidence
  • Prospective study (CEGIR): 15 adults with active EoG/EGE (≥30 eos/hpf)
  • 6-week elemental diet --> complete histological remission (<30 eos/hpf) in:
  • Stomach (p=0.002)
  • Duodenum (p=0.001)
  • 100% of patients achieved remission
  • Improvements in: endoscopic, symptomatic, QoL, molecular measures
  • Food reintroduction --> disease relapse
Elimination Diet Evidence
  • 2006 Chehade study: patients with allergic EoG + anaemia/hypoalbuminaemia
  • Responded to amino acid-based formula
  • Gradual food reintroduction possible over time
  • Many patients still had food-triggered symptoms at 5.5-year follow-up
Practical Considerations
  • All patients should consult with dietitian to avoid nutritional deficiencies
  • Optimal manner and duration of dietary interventions not established
  • Food reintroduction approach needs further study
Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs)
Mechanism
  • Anti-inflammatory effects via inhibition of:
  • Eotaxin-3/CCL26
  • Type 2 cytokines (IL-5, IL-3)
  • Mechanism partly via aryl hydrocarbon receptor
Clinical Use
  • Commonly used off-label for EoG
  • Evidence limited to case reports
  • No randomised controlled trials
Retrospective Study Data (Paediatric)
  • 21 patients <18 years with EoG (>30 eos/hpf in >5 hpfs)
  • Combination first-line: PPI + empiric 1–6 food elimination diet
  • Remission rates:
  • Clinical: 95%
  • Endoscopic: 81%
  • Histological (<20 eos/hpf): 69%
  • Contribution of PPIs to response remains unclear
Leukotriene Receptor Antagonists
Montelukast Sodium
  • Selective leukotriene receptor antagonist
  • Case reports suggest utility as:
  • First-line monotherapy
  • Combined with systemic corticosteroids or ketotifen
  • Steroid-sparing agent
Limitations
  • Risk of neuropsychiatric side effects
  • High-level evidence lacking
Emerging Biologic Therapies
Anti-Siglec-8: Lirentelimab
Phase 2 ENIGMA Trial (NCT03496571)
  • Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled
  • N=65 with EoG/EGE (≥30 eos/hpf in 5 gastric hpfs and/or ≥30 eos/hpf in 3 duodenal hpfs)
  • Results: Mean change in GI eosinophil count:
  • Lirentelimab: –86%
  • Placebo
  • LS mean difference: –98% (95% CI –121 to –76), p<0.001
Phase 3 ENIGMA2 Trial (NCT04322604)
  • N=180 with EoG/EoD
  • Histological co-primary endpoint (≤4 eos/hpf in 5 gastric hpfs and/or ≤15 eos/hpf in 3 duodenal hpfs): MET
  • Symptom co-primary endpoint: NOT MET
  • 84.6% lirentelimab vs 4.5% placebo achieved histological resolution (p<0.0001)
  • No improvement in non-eosinophil indices
Status
  • Development discontinued September 2022 after disappointing phase 3 results
Anti-IL-5/IL-5R: Benralizumab
Phase 2 BEGS Trial (NCT03473977)
  • Single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled
  • N=26 with histologically active EoG (≥30 eos/hpf in ≥5 hpfs), ages 12–60
  • Week 12 results:
  • Benralizumab: 10/13 (77%) achieved remission (<30 eos/hpf)
  • Placebo: 1/13 (8%)
  • Difference: 69% (95% CI 32–85), p=0.001
  • No improvement in non-eosinophil indices
HUDSON GI Study (NCT05251909)
  • Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind
  • Patients aged ≥12 years with EoG/EGE (≥30 eos/hpf in ≥5 hpfs and/or duodenal ≥30 eos/hpf in ≥3 hpfs)
  • STATUS: Terminated prior to completion
Anti-IL-5: Reslizumab and Mepolizumab
Reslizumab Pilot Study
  • 4 patients with EoG + peripheral eosinophilia
  • Single dose resulted in:
  • Mean decrease in AEC: 70% (range 72–94%) at 24 hours
  • Mean decrease: 83% (range 73–94%) at 48 hours
  • Tissue eosinophilia: 50–70% decrease in 3/4 patients
  • Minimal symptom improvement
  • 7–8 weeks post-dose: 2/4 patients had substantial eosinophil increase + symptom worsening
Mepolizumab
  • Case reports suggest utility in EoG patients
  • No ongoing registered trials
Anti-α4β7 Integrin: Vedolizumab
Status
  • Approved for ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease
  • Case reports suggest possible utility in non-EoE EGIDs
  • No ongoing registered trials
Anti-IL-13: Cendakimab
Mechanism
  • Recombinant humanised monoclonal antibody
  • Binds with high affinity to IL-13
  • Inhibits binding to IL-13Rα1 and IL-13Rα2 subunits
Phase 3 Study in EoE
  • Treatment improved symptoms, histology, and endoscopic features vs placebo
Phase 3 Study in EoG (NCT05214768)
  • Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled
  • Japanese adolescents and adults with EoG (≥30 eos/hpf in ≥5 hpfs stomach and/or ≥30 eos/hpf in ≥3 duodenal hpfs)
  • Primary endpoint: Change in mean number of peak eos/hpf from baseline to week 16
  • STATUS: Ongoing
Anti-IL-4/IL-13: Dupilumab
Mechanism
  • Fully human monoclonal antibody targeting shared receptor for IL-4 and IL-13
  • Approved for multiple type 2 inflammatory diseases (including EoE)
Phase 2 DEGAS Trial (NCT03678545)
  • Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled
  • N=41 with histologically active EoG (≥30 eos/hpf in ≥5 hpfs), ages 12–70
  • Primary endpoint: Relative change from baseline in peak eosinophil count at week 12
Week 12 Results
  • LS mean change: –50% (dupilumab) vs –4% (placebo)
  • Difference: –47% (95% CI –70 to –24), p<0.0001
Week 36 Results
  • Improvements maintained or further improved
  • Improved gastric eosinophil counts
  • Improved histopathological, endoscopic, and transcriptomic outcomes
ENGAGE Trial (NCT05831176)
  • Open-label, single-arm, phase 2
  • N=279 with EoG/EoD diagnosis ≥3 months prior
  • Primary endpoint (week 24): Percentage change in peak gastric eosinophil count from baseline
  • Patients receive dupilumab for up to 24 weeks, then eligible for extended treatment (28 more weeks)
  • STATUS: Ongoing
Anti-IgE: Omalizumab
Approved Indications
  • Moderate-to-severe persistent asthma
  • Chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps
  • IgE-mediated food allergy
  • Chronic spontaneous urticaria
EoG Study (NCT00084097)
  • Single-centre, open-label
  • N=9 with EGE (≥25 eos/hpf in gastric or duodenal biopsies)
  • Primary endpoints: Safety + reduction in peripheral AEC at week 16
  • Results: Significant decrease in peripheral AEC by week 16 (p=0.004)
  • Median decrease: 34%
  • Mean decrease: 47%
Subsequent Study
  • Same group --> failed to demonstrate inhibition of allergen-specific Th2 responses
Unmet Needs Summary
Epidemiology
  • Global studies on incidence and prevalence limited
  • Multicentre registries limited
  • Inclusive reporting on demographics needed
Aetiology and Pathogenesis
  • Deeper understanding of pathology and disease triggers required
  • Knowledge gaps: genetic predisposition, molecular pathways
  • Relationship between EoG and hypereosinophilic syndrome needs further study
Diagnosis
  • Disease likely underdiagnosed due to:
  • Limited awareness
  • Misdiagnosis
  • Diagnostic guidelines lacking (adults)
  • Better diagnostic tools needed:
  • Molecular transcriptomics
  • EoG-diagnostic panel development
  • Less invasive tests (blood-based biomarkers) needed
Burden of Disease
  • Specialised medical care lacking
  • Patient-centred outcome measures required for QoL impact understanding
  • Psychosocial aspects should be better recognised
  • Economic impact studies needed
Treatment Options
  • No approved treatments for EoG
  • Consensus treatment guidelines lacking (adults)
  • Well-designed studies supporting existing therapies needed
  • Well-tolerated and effective long-term treatments lacking
  • Agreement on pathological/endoscopic remission criteria missing
  • Most strategies focus on anti-inflammatory rather than root cause reversal
